# Hausdorff dimension of a product with an interval

## Original exercise

Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi, *Real Analysis: Measure Theory,
Integration, and Hilbert Spaces*, Princeton Lectures in Analysis III,
Chapter 7, Problems, exercise 9, printed page 388.
Book DOI: [10.1515/9781400835560](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400835560).

> 9. Let \(E\) be a compact set in \(\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Show that
> \(\dim(E\times I)=\dim(E)+1\), where \(I\) is the unit interval in
> \(\mathbb R\).

## Fixed interpretation and complete target

Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
context.conclusion: dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1, with R^n×R identified with Euclidean R^(n+1), including n=0.

record.type: extended nonnegative diameter of a subset of a metric or extended metric space
record.definition: For a subset A of a metric or extended metric space X, diam(A)=sup{dist(x,y):x,y in A}, using extended distance and sup(empty)=0. For bounded subsets of a Euclidean space it is identified with its finite nonnegative real value; diam(empty)=0.

record.type: scale contents H^s_delta(A) and unnormalized Hausdorff measure H^s(A), valued in [0,infinity]
record.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension.

record.type: library Hausdorff measure, a measure on a Borel extended metric space for each real exponent
record.definition: For an extended metric space X with its Borel measurable structure and real a, μH[a] denotes the native MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure a, defined as mkMetric(r↦r^a). Here mkMetric is the Borel measure associated to the metric outer measure obtained by taking the supremum over positive diameter scales of the outer measures generated by costs on sets of diameter at most that scale. Empty sets have zero cost. This uses the native extended-real-power convention at a=0. Values on arbitrary subsets are outer-measure values. Its explicit countable-cover formula is invoked as a source theorem in the proof.

binders.type: extended metric space with Borel measurable structure

record.type: Hausdorff dimension of a subset of an extended metric space, valued in [0,infinity]
record.definition: dim_H(A) is the native Hausdorff dimension dimH A: with the Borel structure it is sup{a : a is a nonnegative real and μH[a](A)=infinity}, where the supremum is taken in [0,infinity] and sup(empty)=0. Thus dim_H(empty)=0. This is the usual Hausdorff dimension. The proof identifies μH with the supplied unnormalized measure H on Euclidean spaces at every positive exponent; the zero exponent can contribute only the value zero to this supremum.
I=[0,1], with the usual Euclidean distance.

F=E×I. The coordinate identification (x,t)↦(x_1,...,x_n,t) identifies R^n×R with R^(n+1); throughout this product has Euclidean distance sqrt(||x-y||_2^2+|t-u|^2). In particular R^0 is the one-point Euclidean space and this formula also applies when n=0.
D=dim_H(E), initially an extended nonnegative real. Its finiteness is proved before any use of its real value; after that proof it is identified with the corresponding finite nonnegative real.

record.type: Lebesgue measure on the Borel real line
record.definition: λ is Lebesgue measure on R. Write |J|=λ(J), λ|I for its restriction to I, and ∫_I g dλ for the nonnegative (extended-valued) Lebesgue integral with respect to λ|I. Intervals have their usual Lebesgue lengths.

record.statement: For every natural m, subset A⊆R^m and positive real s, H^s(A)=μH[s](A). Consequently: if s>dim_H(A) then H^s(A)=0; if 0<s<dim_H(A) then H^s(A)=infinity; H^s(A)=0 implies dim_H(A)≤s; H^s(A)=infinity implies dim_H(A)≥s. Dimension is nonnegative, including for the empty set.
